title: The Snowball
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes the end-of-lesson pep talk he gives his ninth-grade AP World History students, many of whom meet serious academic difficulty for the first time. His central claim is that steady, daily knowledge acquisition is a slow but compounding strategy, and he tells students to fixate on learning world history rather than on the latest low-stakes quiz. The snowball image carries the argument: knowledge starts small but picks up more the more it is rolled and added to. He frames his two course goals, efficient paths to college credit and enjoying the process, as printed on the syllabus. He also credits a deliberate focus on student motivation and knowledge-building, the subjects of chapters 2 and 3 of his book, for whatever steadiness he has after 13 years. The post is a short, concrete example of how a teacher can reframe difficulty as a knowledge-accumulation process.
points: Difficulty in a demanding course is best met by pointing students at slow, daily accumulation of knowledge instead of at the next quiz or test.
The snowball metaphor makes compounding knowledge visible to students: each new fact makes the next one easier to attach.
Dave pairs the knowledge-building message with an open offer of one-to-one help, so high challenge is matched by support.
He credits a narrow focus on a few things, motivation and knowledge-building, as what keeps his teaching coherent.
quotes: Now mind you, my two goals with every lesson, every assignment, every interaction are to guide my students on the most efficient paths to earning college credit on the AP exam in May AND to teach them how to enjoy the process.

I appreciate many things about the chance to teach the 60-70 kids per year who take this challenge upon themselves, but perhaps my favorite is how the course confronts so many of them, for the first time in their academic lives, with significant difficulty.

Remember: your goal with each night’s work and each day’s lesson is to learn things about world history — as much as you can, but within the time constraints that you have. It’s this slow and steady acquisition and processing and connecting and combining of knowledge, day by day, that forms our very successful and very uncommon strategy.

So rather than fixating on the latest low-stakes quiz or what’s going to be on the test, fixate on learning world history, understanding its patterns, and engaging all-in during the learning exercises we do as a class. And remember that as you go, bit by bit you’re accruing knowledge, and this knowledge acts like a snowball in the winter time — at first it’s small, but the more you roll it around and add to it, the more it’s able to pick up.

My point is that I’m such a poor teacher in so many ways that some days it’s quite disheartening. But I do have the benefit now, 13 years in, of having spent some number of years intently focused on the interplay of six basic things — including student motivation (the five key beliefs) and the critical pursuit of knowledge-building.
